<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Learning Model Representations Using 
<br class="ltx_break">Publicly Available Model Hubs</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Damian Falk
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Konstantin Schürholt
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Konstantinos Tzevelekakis
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Léo Meynent
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Damian Borth
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>AIML Lab,
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>School of Computer Science,
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of St.Gallen
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{first.last}@unisg.ch</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The weights of neural networks have emerged as a novel data modality, giving rise to the field of <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weight space learning</em>.
A central challenge in this area is that learning meaningful representations of weights typically requires large, carefully constructed collections of trained models, typically referred to as <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model zoos</em>. These model zoos are often trained ad-hoc, requiring large computational resources, constraining the learned weight space representations in scale and flexibility.
In this work, we drop this requirement by training a weight space learning backbone on arbitrary models downloaded from large, unstructured model repositories such as Hugging Face. Unlike curated model zoos, these repositories contain highly heterogeneous models: they vary in architecture and dataset, and are largely undocumented. To address the methodological challenges posed by such heterogeneity, we propose a new weight space backbone designed to handle unstructured model populations. We demonstrate that weight space representations trained on models from Hugging Face achieve strong performance, often outperforming backbones trained on laboratory-generated model zoos.
Finally, we show that the diversity of the model weights in our training set allows our weight space model to generalize to unseen data modalities. By demonstrating that high-quality weight space representations can be learned <em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in the wild</em>, we show that curated model zoos are not indispensable, thereby overcoming a strong limitation currently faced by the weight space learning community.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Over the past years, weight space learning (WSL) has emerged as a vibrant research field casting neural-network parameters themselves as a data modality to learn representations from.
WSL aims to learn representations of model weights given a population of models, i.e., a model zoo. Such learned representations can then be exploited for multiple downstream tasks: discriminative (e.g., predicting model properties such as accuracy directly from its weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unterthiner et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eilertsen et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>) or generative (generating new, unseen neural network weights for a given architecture and dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As promising as the exploitation of such learned representations for the above-mentioned downstream tasks is, previously proposed approaches in WSL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unterthiner et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eilertsen et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> share a common limitation: they require trained neural network models as input. Some methods are trained on multiple training checkpoints of a single model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> while others use model zoos (i.e. populations of neural networks that are homogeneous in their training dataset and/or neural network architecture) to train the weight-space backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or a combination of both <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/HuggingSANE_overview_v3.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/133;" width="548" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>An overview of the proposed method. We train a weight space representation directly from the weights of downloaded models from Hugging Face. These models are, to a large extent, undocumented, trained on various datasets, and composed from different neural network architectures. Once a representation is learned from such a heterogeneous model collection, it can be exploited for multiple downstream tasks: either analyzing or generating model weights for multiple architectures and target datasets. Please note, all this is accomplished using the same single representation trained entirely from HF models.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The availability of homogeneous laboratory-trained model zoos therefore represents a major bottleneck: training them demands significant computational resources, particularly when scaling parameter count. And while some recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2025</a>)</cite> suggests using publicly available models from repositories such as Hugging Face (HF), the heterogeneity of neural network models on such platforms is beyond what current methods in WSL are able to train on.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, only <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al. (2024)</a></cite> leverage models taken from HF for weight space learning. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al. (2024)</a></cite> group related models into model trees which can be leveraged for model retrieval and analysis; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al. (2024)</a></cite> use individual models from HF in some experiments. In contrast, our work aims to design a method that can process and learn from <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">arbitrary</span> HF models that are heterogeneous in terms of architecture, training dataset and scale. Further, this work aims to train a single neural representation for all architecture and dataset combinations instead of one individual neural representations per architecture/dataset combination.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Indeed, using the weights of arbitrary models from HF as input for WSL is a non-trivial problem. The learning backbone should (i) handle models trained on different data distributions or tasks, (ii) be scalable to process larger models, and (iii) be able to process and embed different architectures. Additionally, a large fraction of these models are insufficiently documented <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we aim to close this gap and shift WSL from model zoo silos to the open, heterogeneous ecosystem of HF, home to over a million neural network models of different architectures and trained from various datasets. Learning weight space representations to capture the heterogeneity of such a diverse set of neural network models is challenging but potentially possible:  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dravid et al. (2023)</a></cite> showed that different neural networks, composed from different architectures and trained for various vision tasks, share some common representations. Similar is hypothesized by  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al. (2024)</a></cite>, where increased diversity during learning does lead to shared representation spaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Building upon an encoder-decoder transformer architecture  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we propose the first WSL backbone whose training procedure is designed to be agnostic to: (i) model architecture, (ii) training dataset, (iii) model scale, and (iv) input modality for training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we demonstrate that the trained single representation can be used to generate more than 30 different architecture/dataset pairs ranging from ResNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016b</a>)</cite>, ConvNeXts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, EfficientNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan &amp; Le, 2019</a>)</cite> to various transformer models (including ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, Swin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, BeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, GPT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. This practically drops the aforementioned requirement to train on homogeneous model zoos for weight space representation learning.
Summarizing, the contributions of this paper are: (i) training a single weight space representation from arbitrary models downloaded from HF, consisting of 171 billion individual weights, (ii) a novel backbone capable of learning a single task-agnostic and architecture-agnostic representation of weight spaces,
(iii) generalizability in downstream task performance across different datasets and architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Hugging Face Model Collection</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Learning representations of neural network models requires model zoos that are curated and trained in a controlled laboratory environment following a fixed training protocol to collect metadata during training, observe their learning progress, and fully document training trajectories from their start conditions until their converged performance.
More formally, following  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unterthiner et al. (2020)</a></cite>, model zoos are defined as a collection of (converged) neural network models, each being configured by the tuple <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{D},\lambda,\mathcal{A}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{D},\lambda,\mathcal{A}\}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> being the dataset of samples, <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, the set of hyper-parameters used for training, (<span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, loss function, optimizer, learning rate, weight initialization, batch-size, epochs), and <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, a specific neural network architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Downloading neural network models from HF gives us a collection of models where <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{D},\lambda,\mathcal{A}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{D},\lambda,\mathcal{A}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is potentially different for each model in the zoo, and in the worst case where <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is unknown due to a lack of documentation as reported by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Learning a weight space representation from such heterogeneous or even unknown inputs is more challenging than training from laboratory-trained model zoos. One has to deal with unknown dataset distributions, unknown model performance, inconsistent model trajectories, and different architecture families or model trees.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Download Protocol</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To create the HF model collection used in this work, we exploit HF model tags, specifically including ‘image-classification’, ‘image-segmentation’, ‘depth-estimation’, and ‘object-detection’. In total, when querying the HF API with these tags we have <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="22\,055" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>22 055</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">22\,055</annotation></semantics></math> models available, with <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17\,011" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>17 011</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17\,011</annotation></semantics></math> models for ‘image-classification’, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,381" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1 381</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,381</annotation></semantics></math> models for ‘image-segmentation’, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="202" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>202</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">202</annotation></semantics></math> models for ‘depth-estimation’, and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\,461" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3 461</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\,461</annotation></semantics></math> models for ‘object-detection’. We constrained our experimental setup to computer vision models to be comparable to previous works.
For each model in this set, we perform sanity checks: first, we verify if each model can be properly instantiated using the HF auto-classes for model loading, excluding models with missing weights, improperly saved checkpoints, or those requiring remote code execution for initialization. Once instantiated, we attempt to tokenize each model using the tokenization scheme discussed in <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="Tokenization ‣ 3.3 Efficient Model Weight Processing ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>. Successfully tokenized models are kept, and their model IDs are recorded for further processing.
This procedure is done until a subset of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2 000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\,000</annotation></semantics></math> training and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>200</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200</annotation></semantics></math> validation models is retrieved.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">HF Model Collection</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An overview of the composition of the retrieved HF model collection can be seen in Fig.<a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Specifically, the included models fall under the families of Transformer (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="42.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>42.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">42.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>), ConvNet (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="21.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>21.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>) and hybrid (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math>) architectures. Notably, a large percentage of these model architectures (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="31.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>31.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">31.4\%</annotation></semantics></math>) does not provide any information in the name and is classified as unknown. The composition of the collection is further analyzed into ResNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016a</a>)</cite>, ConvNeXT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, EfficientNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan &amp; Le, 2019</a>)</cite>, ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, SwinTransformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>, BeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, DeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and other architectures. Interestingly, half of the model collection appears to be trained on variations of ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, whereas for the other half of the collection no information is provided. In the end, our HF model collection contains in total 171 billion individual parameters to be used for WSL.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To accomplish training on uncurated models from HF, we require a learning backbone capable of scaling to arbitrary model sizes and capable of processing heterogeneous neural network architectures. Currently, no learning backbone would match these requirements (we discuss this in more detail in App. <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Weight Space Backbones ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). On the one hand, some existing learning backbones are able to scale but fail to process heterogeneous model architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. SANE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> requires homogeneous architectures of models in the zoo for the layer-wise loss normalization, p-diff <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and RPG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> require checkpoints saved during the training process of a single model. On the other hand, there are methods that can process heterogeneous architectures but are not able to scale at the same time. For instance, with D2NWG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>)</cite> a unified backbone can only be trained on classifier-heads and small models. Therefore, our method bridges this gap in the literature by training a single weight-space representation on arbitrary models at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While differing in their specific implementation, all these works have something in common: they are based on an encoder-decoder learning backbone which we also build upon. Specifically, we base our work on the encoder-decoder transformer setup of SANE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminary: the <span id="S3.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SANE</span> backbone</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SANE is an autoencoder where both the encoder and the decoder are symmetric transformers. Given some input NN weights <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=[\bm{W_{1}},...,\bm{W_{l}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒍</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=[\bm{W_{1}},...,\bm{W_{l}}]</annotation></semantics></math> where the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the weight matrices for the different layers, we first tokenize them as a sequence of tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},...,\bm{t_{n}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒏</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},...,\bm{t_{n}}]</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{t_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{t_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the individual tokens (cf. <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="Tokenization ‣ 3.3 Efficient Model Weight Processing ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> for more details about the tokenization). We then pass them through the encoder <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to embed them into a lower dimensional latent representation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}(\bm{T})=\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}(\bm{T})=\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>, before the decoder <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> reconstructs the tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\psi}(\bm{Z})=\bm{\hat{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\psi}(\bm{Z})=\bm{\hat{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>. To train this autoencoder, a combination of two losses is used. First, a contrastive loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2020</a>)</cite> is used in the latent representation space, using augmentations such as permutations, noise and masking. Second, an MSE loss on <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T}</annotation></semantics></math> and its reconstruction <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\hat{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\hat{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
After training, the encoder can be used to embed unknown models into the latent representation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> for discriminative downstream tasks such as accuracy or hyperparameter prediction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Alternatively, by sampling new representations <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{Z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{Z}}</annotation></semantics></math> and passing them through the decoder, one can generate synthetic tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{T}}=h_{\psi}(\bm{\tilde{Z}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{T}}=h_{\psi}(\bm{\tilde{Z}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which can then be detokenized into neural network weights <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}</annotation></semantics></math>. To sample from the latent representations <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{Z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{Z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, SANE uses one or multiple trained neural network models (tokenized as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑻</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>) as <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anchors</em> to sample <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{Z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{Z}}</annotation></semantics></math> in the vicinity of their latent representations <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z_{a}}=g_{\theta}(\bm{T_{a}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒁</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑻</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z_{a}}=g_{\theta}(\bm{T_{a}})</annotation></semantics></math>. We discuss the different components of this learning backbone in more detail in <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 SANE ‣ Appendix B Weight Space Backbones ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To enable such an encoder-decoder learning backbone to learn a weight space representation from diverse architectures included in the HF model collection, significant modifications to the backbone are required. In the following, we outline these changes, including the design choices and implementation details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Masked Loss Normalization (MLN)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Previous WSL work established that different weight distributions between different layers present a challenge for weight representation learning  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
As remedies, they propose to either normalize the weights per layer across the entire dataset as a preprocessing step, or normalize the loss contribution accordingly. Both approaches present challenges for large, inhomogeneous weight datasets. They are not immediately applicable for varying architectures since they compute normalizations per layer and thus require matching architectures. Further, such normalizations may fail for models trained on different computer vision datasets with different weight distributions. Normalizing the loss per layer inherits these constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To tackle this challenge, we propose to normalize loss contributions <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">per-token</span> at runtime. This has two benefits: (i) it simplifies the normalization and operates across different model architectures and weight distributions, (ii) the representation learning model still operates in weight space, which simplifies evaluating weight generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We normalize each original token <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{t_{i}}\in\bm{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝑻</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{t_{i}}\in\bm{T}</annotation></semantics></math> and its predicted reconstruction <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\widehat{t_{i}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\widehat{t_{i}}}</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau_{i}}=\frac{\bm{t_{i}}-\bar{t}}{\sigma_{t}},\quad\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}=\frac{\bm{\widehat{t_{i}}}-\bar{t}}{\sigma_{t}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau_{i}}=\frac{\bm{t_{i}}-\bar{t}}{\sigma_{t}},\quad\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}=\frac{\bm{\widehat{t_{i}}}-\bar{t}}{\sigma_{t}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are the mean and standard deviation of calculated over the current batch of tokens. Depending on the tokenization strategy used, tokens may includes zero-padding to harmonize token size, which can skew the mean and standard deviation estimators. We therefore ensure that both these estimators only take unmasked elements into account. When then compute the reconstruction mean-squared error loss between the normalized tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\widehat{\tau_{i}}}</annotation></semantics></math>. MLN is conceptually similar to normalization layers in neural networks. While normalization layers stabilize training by standardizing activations before they are passed forward, the goal of MLN is to stabilize weight-space representation learning by re-centering and rescaling tokens before their reconstruction error is computed. In both cases, normalization removes scale-related biases and ensures that optimization focuses on the relative structure of the representation rather than raw magnitudes, enabling more robust learning across heterogeneous architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Efficient Model Weight Processing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Below we outline our adaptations NN weight tokenization and encoding their structure to be processed by the WSL backbone, with a focus processing diverse architectures and reducing memory overhead to enable training of a <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">single</span> weight space representation instead of training multiple representations for different settings.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tokenization</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To effectively train an autoencoder on neural network parameters, there are two main approaches followed in the literature. The works of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al. (2024)</a></cite> represent neural networks as graphs and use graph neural networks to process them. Other approaches flatten the entire neural network into a 1D vector before processing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite> additionally using a VQ-VAE model to generate discrete token representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Further splitting the flattened weights into tokens of a fixed size has been proposed in SANE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to address scaling issues with embedding larger architectures. SANE follows a tokenization approach in which the parameters of the model are divided into chunks that are later processed by an autoencoder. Given neural network weights <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=[\bm{W_{1}},\ldots,\bm{W_{l}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒍</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=[\bm{W_{1}},\ldots,\bm{W_{l}}]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the weight matrix of the <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th layer, each <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> lies in <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{1}\times\cdots\times c_{\textnormal{in}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo><mo lspace="0.055em" rspace="0.055em">⋯</mo><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{1}\times\cdots\times c_{\textnormal{in}}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> representing the number of channels. Each <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> is flattened into a 2D matrix <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{r}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{r}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="c_{r}=c_{1}\cdot\cdots\cdot c_{\textnormal{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0.055em" rspace="0.055em">⋯</mo><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{r}=c_{1}\cdot\cdots\cdot c_{\textnormal{in}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The weights are then sliced row-wise, along the outgoing channel dimension, and each resulting vector is partitioned into tokens <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒕</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of length <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}\nmid c_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∤</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}\nmid c_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>, the final token is zero-padded to length <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The full token sequence is obtained as <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},\ldots,\bm{t_{n}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒏</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},\ldots,\bm{t_{n}}]</annotation></semantics></math>, constructed by stacking all tokens from all weight matrices in order.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Depending on the number of weights per channel in the individual layers, this often leads to very <em id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sparse</em> tokens that include a significant portion of zero-pads. This is especially pronounced when tokenizing diverse architectures as the token size cannot be optimized to minimize the amount of padding required for that single architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As these pads still take up space in memory and need to be processed, they represent an obstacle in scaling up the learning backbone to larger architectures and more diverse models. To address this limitation, we explore using a <em id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dense</em> tokenization instead, similarly to what  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite> developed in parallel to our work. In that case, for every <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{1}\times...\times c_{\textnormal{in}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{out}}\times c_{1}\times...\times c_{\textnormal{in}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we flatten it to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X_{i}^{\textnormal{flat}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{flat}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>𝒊</mi><mtext>flat</mtext></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>flat</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X_{i}^{\textnormal{flat}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textnormal{flat}}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textnormal{flat}}=c_{\textnormal{out}}*c_{1}*...*c_{\textnormal{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>flat</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textnormal{flat}}=c_{\textnormal{out}}*c_{1}*...*c_{\textnormal{in}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We then cut the resulting vector <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X_{i}^{\textnormal{flat}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>𝒊</mi><mtext>flat</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X_{i}^{\textnormal{flat}}}</annotation></semantics></math> into tokens <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒕</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of length <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}\nmid c_{\textnormal{flat}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∤</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>flat</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}\nmid c_{\textnormal{flat}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we zero-pad the last token to length <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, before concatenating all tokens for all layers in order to obtain <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},...,\bm{t_{n}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒕</mi><mi>𝒏</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T}=[\bm{t_{1}},...,\bm{t_{n}}]</annotation></semantics></math>. Given that we zero-pad per layer, and not per outgoing channel anymore, the amount of padding is much lower. In <a href="#A4.SS4.SSS2" title="D.4.2 Tokenization ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4.2</span></a>, we explore the impact of dense and sparse tokenization on token sparsity, memory footprint and model performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sinusoidal Positional Encoding</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because the backbone is based on the transformer architecture, positional encodings are required to represent the sequential structure of the input data. In our case, token positions are represented with a three-dimensional vector <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{P}=[n,l,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑷</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{P}=[n,l,k]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the position of the token in the full model sequence, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the layer index, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to the token position within the layer. SANE uses learned positional embeddings which in our case is not feasible given the diversity and scale of the downloaded HF dataset. Particularly, the number of parameters required for learned positional embeddings grows with the sequence length of the flattened weights, leading to a significant memory overhead when scaling to larger architectures included in our training set. The SANE backbone trained on ResNet-18 models contains ~865M trainable parameters out of which ~57M are used for the position embedding with a max dimension of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{P}=[55000,100,550]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑷</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>55000,100,550</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{P}=[55000,100,550]</annotation></semantics></math>. In our case the resulting embedding matrix would become significantly larger as the HF trainset contains models with up to 1.3B parameters compared to ~12M params of a ResNet-18 (see <a href="#A4.SS4.SSS2" title="D.4.2 Tokenization ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4.2</span></a> for more details). To solve this issue, we replace learned positional embeddings with sinusoidal positional encodings  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite> which provide a parameter-free approach for encoding position. This inherently scale-invariant method can efficiently support models of varying sizes, allowing the backbone to capture relative positions which are of utmost importance in our heterogeneous WSL context by exploiting the linear relationship between the sinusoidal positional encodings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this Section, we test our training pipeline using models from the HF model collection (Sec. <a href="#S2" title="2 Hugging Face Model Collection ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) as training data. First, we assess the methodological adaptations described in <a href="#S3" title="3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We then evaluate the proposed method as a whole, hypothesizing that with an increasing amount of training samples from HF the trained backbone is able to compensate potential noisiness in our HF model collection when compared to training with laboratory-trained model zoos. To that end, we directly compare our approach to SANE, but unlike SANE which trains individual weight space representations for each architecture-dataset pair, we train a single representation across HF models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We design our experiments to run on a single H100 GPU. Training hyperparameters and time as well as implementation details for all experiments are detailed in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on generative downstream tasks and include discriminative results in <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Discriminative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>. For the evaluation of our generative capabilities we test the performance of generated models either without any updates of trainable parameters or with a few epochs of finetuning. Our interest lies in exploring whether our backbone is able to learn a lower dimensional representation from HF models. To that end we use the <span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">subsampling</span> method introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2024)</a></cite> as detailed in <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 SANE ‣ Appendix B Weight Space Backbones ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.
Please note that for all outlined experiments above, we use a single backbone to generate model weights instead of individually trained backbones as done in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Masked Loss Normalization (MLN)</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the first experiment, we focus on validating the core methodological changes introduced in this work, aiming to assess their impact on representation quality, convergence stability, and general performance. We focus on the Masked Loss Normalization (MLN) and provide further ablations on the tokenization scheme and positional encodings in <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>. We evaluate whether the masked loss normalization allows the backbone to adequately capture the different weight distributions of different layers and models which has been shown to be problematic when not normalizing the weights layer wise before training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This is crucial, since the encoder-decoder approach proposed as backbone operates directly in weight space, where skewed or squashed distributions - even of just individual layers - can have a catastrophic impact on the performance of generated models. To validate the proposed loss normalization, we train the backbone on ResNet-18 models from the model zoo dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022c</a>)</cite> and generate models for three different datasets to compare the proposed masked loss normalization (MLN) to the baseline in isolation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss normalization at runtime allows training without global weight normalization during pre-processing</h5>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>
Accuracy of generated ResNet-18 models. We compare SANE with layer-wise loss normalization (LWLN) as baseline with the performance when training with the proposed masked loss normalization (MLN).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiment demonstrates that training with masked loss normalization is a suitable replacement for global weight normalization at dataset preprocessing time. Further, we did not encounter training instabilities, which might have been introduced for padding-heavy tokens. These experiments confirm transformer based encoder-decoder backbones such as SANE can be trained with the proposed masked loss normalization allowing training on arbitrary architectures given the same token size. Compared to the baseline (<a href="#S4.T1" title="In Loss normalization at runtime allows training without global weight normalization during pre-processing ‣ 4.1 Masked Loss Normalization (MLN) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) our approach outperforms SANE on CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet, while showing slightly worse performance on CIFAR10. We include further analysis and discussion in <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
