<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>
Accuracy of generated ResNet-18 models when restricting the HF model collection to specific architecture groups compared to training on HF models in the category computer vision. Three additional subsets of the model collection including only specific architecture groups are created for backbone training. Num models refers to the number of models that are tokenized in the trainset (90% of available models) since we use 10% of the models for the validation set. Num tokens refers to the approximate number of tokens in the training dataset when using dense tokenization with tokensize 230.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To gain insights into how the composition of the HF training set influences downstream performance and whether such a training set-up is feasible, we systematically vary the diversity and scale of the models included in the HF model collection. In particular, we compare training on broad heterogeneous collections against subsets restricted to specific architecture families. In addition to the main HF model collection (<a href="#S2" title="2 Hugging Face Model Collection ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) we create three subsets of our HF model collection, each restricted to a single family of NN architectures: ResNet, ConvNext, and ViT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The ResNet and ConvNeXt subsets of our HF model collection include 360 and 306 models respectively, as there are fewer models on HF including those specific keywords in the name. Only the vision transformer subset is filled to 2000 models. Please note that the number of models in the dataset does not directly translate to the number of tokens, as that is also dependent on the model size. Therefore we use the number of tokens as a proxy for dataset size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The results are included in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Impact of HF Model Collection Composition ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and show increasingly improved performance when including more models for training of the backbone even if they are not representative of the target architecture generated during inference. The performance of generated models when training the backbone on ResNets from HF is close to random guessing for CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet. When training on HF ConvNext models, the performance of the generated methods is above random guessing across all datasets, but remains low. The backbone trained only on vision transformers is able to outperform the others even though we generate ResNet-18 models and not ViTs, simply because it includes much more samples. Training on the full vision dataset leads to a performance plateau: improving on CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet while showing slightly worse performance on CIFAR100. We run further ablations on HF model collection size in <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/hf_backbone_scale.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:220/139;" width="220" height="139" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Accuracy of generated ResNet-18 models on the respective target image datasets. No trainable parameters are updated before the performance evaluation. We compare training on homogeneous model zoos using SANE with MLN, to training the backbone on HF models. HF (S) and HF (L) designate the small and large versions of the backbone, respectively. With the exception of CIFAR-10, our approach outperforms model zoo training for all datasets.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Generating Weights for Varying Datasets</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the next experiment, we include a broader evaluation across a variety of downstream datasets. In addition to CIFAR10 (C10), CIFAR100 (C100) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky &amp; Hinton, 2009</a>)</cite>, and TinyImageNet (TIN) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le &amp; Yang, 2015</a>)</cite>, we generate model weights for SVHN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Netzer et al., 2011</a>)</cite> and EuroSAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Helber et al., 2019</a>)</cite> while keeping the architecture fixed to a ResNet-18. We compare to SANE with MLN trained on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 model zoos as baseline. Given the results from the previous experiment, we hypothesize that this is due to the vision dataset being too large for our backbone configuration and, therefore, run an additional experiment where we scale the backbone. Specifically, we train a small variation (~450M params) as before and a large variation (~900M params) which is comparable to SANE (~865M params). The results (<a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.2 Impact of HF Model Collection Composition ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) show improved performance albeit at the cost of longer training time. Compared to the baseline, we observe lower performance on CIFAR10 but higher performance across all other tested datasets when generated with the large HF trained backbone. We analyze whether the increased training time when scaling the backbone is an acceptable tradeoff by generating a wider variety of architectures in the next experiment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Generating Weights for varying Architectures</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/architecture_group_performance_with_overall.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/170;" width="548" height="170" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Accuracy of generated models on ImageNet-1K after a few epochs of finetuning. We show the performance of three different architecture types as well as the overall mean<math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>std accuracy over all generated models comparing to training from scratch.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established that it is feasible to use HF models as training data, we are interested in the scalability of our proposed approach. In particular, we want to find out whether through the increased heterogeneity of our training dataset we are able to generate models for a wider variety of architectures compared to the baseline. For this, we reverse the generation procedure: we keep the downstream dataset fixed to ImageNet-1K and generate different architectures using the Timm library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wightman, 2019</a>)</cite> to instantiate models, which greatly simplifies the finetuning and evaluation pipeline. In total, we generate weights for 25 different architectures ranging from ResNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016b</a>)</cite>, ConvNeXts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, EfficientNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan &amp; Le, 2019</a>)</cite> to various transformer models (including ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, Swin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, BeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, GPT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2018</a>)</cite>) and more. The full list of generated architectures is included in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> including the hyperparameters used to finetune the models. In Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Generating Weights for varying Architectures ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> we show the results for selected architecture types as well as the mean<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>std accuracy over all generated models compared to training the model with the exact same configuration from scratch. Full results for each architecture are included in <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/validation_comparison_v4.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:220/192;" width="220" height="192" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Comparing a generated GPT-2 model on OpenWebText to training from scratch. Results show the performance on the minival split and indicate that our backbone can generalize to a different modality showing improved performance over standard weight init.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results show that our backbone is able to generate a wide variety of architectures with significant and consistent performance gains over training from scratch. However, the benefit is only visible when finetuning the models: the initial performance remains slightly above or at random guessing. This is inline with previous findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meynent et al., 2025</a>)</cite> showing that generated weights or learned weight updates can introduce small impurities that have a catastrophic impact on initial performance when scaling to larger architectures and more complex datsets. This can generally be fixed with a few optimization steps using standard SGD-based optimizers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As baseline we train our backbone on ResNet-18 models from the CIFAR10 model zoo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022c</a>)</cite>. Here we include all proposed adaptations from <a href="#S3" title="3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> as otherwise scaling to larger architectures is not feasible. The results show that SANE remains competitive when the generated architecture is similar to the training data (e.g., ResNet or small ConvNeXt models), but struggles to scale to larger or more distinct architectures. Likewise, smaller backbones show diminishing or negligible gains over training from scratch as model size increases. Full results are provided in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.4.1 </span>Generating Weights for out of distribution tasks</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further test whether our representation that was trained only on vision models is able to generate weights for the initialization of a GPT-2 language model (~125M parameters) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. We finetune the model on OpenWebText <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gokaslan et al., 2019</a>)</cite> to assess initial trends. We show the validation loss, perplexity, accuracy, and F1 score of the generated model compared to training from scratch. Results (<a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.4 Generating Weights for varying Architectures ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) show that our backbone is able to generate weights that converge faster, even though we restrict the HF dataset to computer vision models. While we cannot guarantee that the HF dataset does not include weights of models trained jointly with language embeddings (e.g., through CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite>), this result indicates that the learned representation is able to generalize to a different modality.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advancements in representation learning for neural network weights have introduced various methods for analyzing and generating model weights. Hyper-Representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>)</cite> employ an encoder-decoder framework with contrastive guidance to learn weight representations for property prediction and model generation. Alternatively, some methods use diffusion on weights for generation purposes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Graph-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Neural Functionals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and related approaches like Deep Weight Space (DWS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> learn equivariant or invariant representations of weights. In conjunction with backbone architectures, data augmentations have been proposed to improve generalization of WSL methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shamsian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Other approaches focus on probing intermediate layers of neural network to predict attributes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Also related are HyperNetworks, which directly use the underlying data and labels to guide the weights-generation signal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brock et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Our work focuses on the autoencoder-based approaches due to their broad applicability across various architectures and downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we have shown that training weight space models does not necessarily require laboratory-generated model zoos, which are expensive to train, take large amounts of storage and are therefore difficult to share with the larger community. Instead, we show the strong potential in training weight space models using publicly available model weights from repositories such as Hugging Face. This opens up multiple avenues for future work. First, our exploration has focused on a limited number of computer vision models. The training set of model weights from HF could be extended both in size and diversity by adding more models and covering more data modalities. Second, we have not applied manual curation beyond basic feasibility checks, meaning that the subset of models we train on may not fully represent the much larger pool of available weights. This raises the possibility of selection bias that could impact performance. While our goal is precisely to enable training on arbitrary, heterogeneous collections of models rather than carefully curated zoos, future work could further investigate how such biases may arise and to what extent they affect robustness. Finally, by leveraging models as diverse as those from HF, our work marks a significant step towards applying weight space models to downstream tasks, for which no model zoo is available.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Conclusion</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to overcome the need of model zoos, one of the limitations faced by the WSL community. To do so, we have first described how we collected models from the HF repository. We have then adapted an existing WSL backbone to work on our dataset, and have validated that our adaptations work and are good performance-efficiency trade-offs. We have then demonstrated though a variety of experiments that training a single autoencoder on HF data shows superior or similar levels of performance compared to SANE autoencoders trained on individual architecture-dataset pairs. Furthermore, we have shown that our single model displays good generalization performance, being able to generate good initialization weights for an out-of-distribution GPT-2 model. Through these results, we demonstrate that training on model weights found <em id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in the wild</em> is as good as, but often better, than on laboratory-generated model zoos, and it is both more general and more efficient. This finding makes the training of weight space models more accessible, and opens up exciting new opportunities in the development of methods and applications in WSL.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

</div>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Weight Space Backbones</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Choice of the Weight Space Backbone</h3>

<figure id="A2.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>
Summary of the capabilities of different weight-space methods. <sup id="A2.T3.5" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>By data agnostic, we express that the weight-space method does not need the data used to train the model weights it trains on. <sup id="A2.T3.6" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>By architecture agnostic, we express that the weight-space method does not need any knowledge of the model architecture, only the weights. <sup id="A2.T3.7" class="ltx_sup">3</sup>We show which methods can be used to generate synthetic neural network weights.</figcaption>

<td id="A2.T3.8.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">✓</td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T3.8.7" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T3.8.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">Hyper-Representations</th>
<td id="A2.T3.8.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">✓</td>
<td id="A2.T3.8.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">~</td>
<td id="A2.T3.8.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">✓</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this Section, we explore different weight space backbones from the literature and evaluate how fit they are for our use-case. In particular, they should be capable of handling heterogeneous, often poorly documented <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2025</a>)</cite> models from the HF repository <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hugging Face, Inc. (2025)</a></cite>. This is critical since we cannot directly filter models based on performance or other attributes unless we constrain our dataset creation to the smaller subset of labeled models. We summarize the capabilities of existing weight-space backbones in <a href="#A2.T3" title="In B.1 Choice of the Weight Space Backbone ‣ Appendix B Weight Space Backbones ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. There, we show that most of the existing weight-space backbones come with inherent limitations. Simple weight statistics have been shown to be very cheap and effective for discriminative downstream tasks such as predicting model performance and hyper-parameters, they can be used in a way that is architecture agnostic, but they are not adapted for neural network weights generation. DWSNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and graph-based backbones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2024</a>)</cite> use different approaches to encode the inherent symmetries and structures of neural networks, making them by definition dependent on the underlying models’ architecture. Functionalist methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Herrmann et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meynent et al., 2025</a>)</cite> that focus on the models’ outputs rather than their weights can easily be made architecture agnostic but rely on relevant data samples for probing and are, therefore, not data agnostic. Existing diffusion-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for neural network weight generation are currently not completely architecture agnostic. More specifically, both the diffusion model and the learning backbone are usually trained for a single network architecture at a time, in particular when scaling to larger architectures. This limitation also prevents these approaches from being fully dataset- and task-agnostic, since the architecture is usually tied to both the task and the dataset and often requires additional labeled data for conditioning that is not available for most HF models. Finally, the SANE backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, while not entirely architecture agnostic, can be adapted to be with some targeted changes; it can also perform neural network weights generation. For these reasons, we base our work on the SANE architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>SANE</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we provide additional details about the Sequential Autoencoder for Neural Embeddings (SANE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> method and approach.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Pre-Processing and Tokenization</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before training the model-zoos need to be sliced into tokens to allow scaling the hyper-representation to larger model-zoos. The required steps are described below.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layer wise loss normalization</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2022a)</a></cite> mention that due to the reconstruction loss being based on a mean squared error, the hyper-representation will learn to reconstruct the weights to evenly spread the reconstruction error across all weights and layers in the weight vector (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>). However, the distribution of weight magnitudes can differ significantly between layers and also between different models even if they share the same architecture. This can lead to an issue where layers with large-magnitude weights and broader distributions are reconstructed accurately, but those with smaller magnitudes and narrow distributions can be neglected. This imbalance can make these smaller-weight layers a weak point in the reconstructed models, which can lead to a severe drop in performance, sometimes as low as random guessing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2022a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2024)</a></cite>. They therefore propose to normalize the weights of the input model-zoo as a first step. The weights are normalized with the mean (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>) and standard deviation (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>) calculated per layer throughout the whole model zoo. However, as outlined in <a href="#S3" title="3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> this is not feasible when training on diverse architectures with varying depth and width without significant engineering overhead and why we propose the masked loss normalization at runtime instead which greatly simplifies pre-processing and evaluation while achieving comparable results.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tokenization</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The weights are reshaped into 2D matrices and sliced row-wise along the outgoing channels (which we refer to in the paper as <span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sparse</span> tokenization). These slices are divided into multiple parts based on a predefined token size (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>). If a slice does not fill an entire token, zero padding is applied to reach the required token size. Each token is then augmented with a 3-dimensional positional embedding, as explained in <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="Tokenization ‣ 3.3 Efficient Model Weight Processing ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Windowing</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the complete sequence of tokens and their positional embeddings, a random subset is selected, consisting of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> consecutive tokens up to a specified window size (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ws" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ws</annotation></semantics></math>). The model is trained using these windows, enabling it to handle large models by focusing on manageable segments at a time. During training, one window is sampled per model, ensuring that a batch contains tokens from different models. This also allows to draw different windows at each training iteration to further mitigate the risk of over-fitting. By decoupling the computational requirements from the input model size, SANE can scale to any architecture, regardless of its size. Through the tokenization process, it is also possible to train on different input architectures simultaneously as long as they are preprocessed and sliced into the same token and window size. For our experiments we preprocess the models into windows of tokens of length 4096 out of which a random subset of 512 tokens is sampled during each training iteration to reduce the risk of overfitting and improving training time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Augmentations</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original SANE implementation uses three different data augmentations in the context of its contrastive loss: masking, additive white gaussian noise and permutations. For the latter, the authors leverage the existing symmetries in neural networks that make it possible to swap the order of neurons without changing the input-output function of the model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainsworth et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hecht-Nielsen (1990)</a></cite>. When using model weights from HF that are not properly documented, it is not possible to know which permutations conserve this input-output function without knowledge about the architecture. For this reason, we do not explicitly deal with the symmetries of the models in our dataset, and only use the masking and noising augmentations to investigate whether it is still possible to achieve comparable performance to previous work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.2 </span>Downstream Tasks</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SANE is a unified model and approach for discriminative and generative downstream tasks. The following paragraphs briefly introduce the methods used for both task families.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discriminative Tasks</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For discriminative downstream tasks, one can pass a set of tokens <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T}</annotation></semantics></math> representing a model’s weights through the SANE encoder <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain a latent representation <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}(\bm{T})=\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}(\bm{T})=\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>. The latent representations is then averaged over all tokens to a single vector <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\bar{Z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\bar{Z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is processed with a linear probe or a Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict model properties. These include as accuracy, loss, generalization gap, training epoch, model-zoo, etc. The predictive performance of the linear probe/MLP can be measured in terms of explained variance (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) on the test set in the case of a regression (e.g., accuracy with continuous values) or in terms of accuracy in the case of classification (e.g., prediction of the architecture of the embedded model).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative Sampling of Models</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SANE is also able to sample models directly out of the representation space. The difficulty lies in identifying the distribution <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(\bm{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\bm{Z})</annotation></semantics></math> of the latent representation space that can be decoded to a functional NN in the target domain. SANE uses a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to model the target distribution <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(\bm{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\bm{Z})</annotation></semantics></math> by tokenizing a few <em id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anchors</em> <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{T_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑻</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{T_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> and projecting them to the latent space using the encoder <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z_{a}}=g_{\theta}(\bm{T_{a}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒁</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑻</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z_{a}}=g_{\theta}(\bm{T_{a}})</annotation></semantics></math>. The resulting KDE over the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒁</mi><mi>𝒂</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> is then broadly sampled to identify regions in the distribution with high probability of the desired target properties. The sampled representations <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{Z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{Z}}</annotation></semantics></math> are passed through the decoder <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> to generate synthetic tokens <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tilde{T}}=h_{\psi}(\bm{\tilde{Z}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑻</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tilde{T}}=h_{\psi}(\bm{\tilde{Z}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which can then be detokenized into neural network weights <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Batch Norm Conditioning</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Larger models often include batch norm layers that in part contain parameters that are not trained via backpropagation and are only updated during the forward pass. Since the distribution of these weights differs significantly from trainable parameters, they are excluded from sampling. Instead, batch norm conditioning is performed, which updates (only non-trainable) parameters during a few forward passes on the target dataset to align these parameters with the trainable weights before evaluating the accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Haloing</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Optionally, SANE allows for the use of haloing, where context weights are added before and after the window before processing by the encoder. This added context is processed normally but disregarded after reconstruction by the decoder.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</section>

<td id="A3.T4.1.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;"><math id="A3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2e-5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2e-5</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A3.T4.1.11.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;"><math id="A3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2e-5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2e-5</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<tr id="A3.T4.1.12" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T4.1.12.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;">weight decay</th>
<td id="A3.T4.1.12.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;"><math id="A3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3e-9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3e-9</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A3.T4.1.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;"><math id="A3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3e-9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3e-9</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A3.T4.1.12.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:12.0pt;padding-right:12.0pt;"><math id="A3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3e-9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3e-9</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T4.1.13" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>
Implementation Details for Hugging Face Training and Baseline
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we provide additional information on the training hyper-parameters and architecture configuration of the two HF trained backbones (HF-Small and HF-Large) as well as for testing our masked loss normalization (MLN) on model-zoo data (SANE MLN). We keep the baseline experimental set-up to validate the MLN as close as possible to the original SANE implementation in order for the results to be comparable. For training on HF data we introduce additional changes to the model size, number of training epochs and number of layers to balance the trade-off between performance and efficiency. We train the small backbone (HF-Small) for 100 epochs for comparing dense and sparse tokenization as well as for the ablations (<a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>) to reduce training time. For comparing to the large backbone (HF-Large) we also train the small backbone for 300 epochs (<a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>) for evaluating across different architectures. The SANE baseline evaluated on ImageNet-1K is trained according to the HF-Small configuration for 100 epochs as we observed degrading performance when training for longer on homogeneous model zoos.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>List of generated models</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For our experiments across different datasets we use ResNet-18 models from publicly available model zoo datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Honegger et al., 2023</a>)</cite> with the exception of SVHN where we train 5 models from scratch. Below we list all generated architectures from the Timm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wightman, 2019</a>)</cite> library that we finetune on ImageNet-1K. We organize the models in architecture groups and specify the sampled architectures within that group. The specific instance of the timm model used is specified within parentheses.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">

<li id="A3.I1.i9" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Swin</p>
<ul id="A3.I1.i9.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Swin S3 Tiny (swin_s3_tiny_224.ms_in1k)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i9.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Finetuning params</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the same training pipeline for all finetuned models and only vary the batch size for the larger models (256 instead of 512). For generating weights we use haloing with an added context of 2*64 tokens per window (of size 512) and batch-norm conditioning. For our experiment on ImageNet we use one anchor sample from Timm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wightman, 2019</a>)</cite> and sample five models per architecture and finetune the best one. For sampling different datasets we use 5 anchor samples per target dataset and sample 50 models and keep the top 10. For data augmentations we use a random resized crop and random horizontal flip and normalize with the ImageNet mean and standard deviation. For validation we use rescaling with a center crop as well as normalization. We finetune the models for 5 epochs using the Adam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma, 2014</a>)</cite> optimizer with learning rate <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e-3</annotation></semantics></math> with autocast and gradient scaling. For sampling across different datasets we show the performance of sampled models without any finetuning of trainable parameters using the same augmentations as in the respective model zoo. The configuration and finetuning hyperparameters for the GPT-2 model are summarized in <a href="#A3.T5" title="In C.2 Finetuning params ‣ Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Results &amp; Ablations</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we include detailed results for our generative (<a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>) and discriminative (<a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Discriminative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>) downstream tasks. We also include full results for the baselines in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Generative Results</h3>

<section id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Full results per architecture</h5>

<div id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A4.T6" title="In Full results per architecture ‣ D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> we report the mean<math id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>std performance of all sampled models after 1-5 epochs of finetuning. As baselines, we include SANE trained on CIFAR10 with loss normalization and sinusoidal positional encodings, as well as models trained from scratch. Further below we show the individual results per sampled architecture after 1-5 epochs of finetuning comparing to training from scratch. Specifically, we show the performance of the large backbone in <a href="#A4.T7" title="In Full results per architecture ‣ D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and the performance of the small backbone in <a href="#A4.T8" title="In Full results per architecture ‣ D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. The results of our baseline per architecture are included in <a href="#A4.T10" title="In D.3.2 Architectures ‣ D.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Mean<math id="A4.T6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>std performance of generated models per backbone in percent after 1-5 epochs of finetuning. The results are calculated over all sampled models and show that training on HF models outperforms previous work trained on homogenous model zoos when scaling to larger and more diverse architectures. While the baseline achieves competitive results for architectures that are close to the training set (i.e. ResNets or ConvNexts) performance drops for other architectures and often leads to worse performance than training from scratch. Conversely, our HF trained backbones are able to consistently outperform training from scratch. The large backbone improves upon the small backbone in particular for larger sampled architectures.</figcaption>

<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Discriminative Results</h3>

<figure id="A4.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Discriminative results on the ResNet-18 model-zoos. The results show explained variance (<math id="A4.T9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) per target dataset. A linear probe fits the embeddings to the target properties of the respective trainset and the performance on the testset is reported. For the evaluation the ResNet-18 model zoos from the model zoo dataset are used <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022c</a>)</cite>. 100 models are split into train/test/validation with proportions 70/15/15 using checkpoints from epochs 1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25.</figcaption>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A4.T9" title="In D.2 Discriminative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> we evaluate whether the embeddings of the encoder trained on HF-data are still predictive of model properties as was shown in previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We observe a performance drop compared to previous work in all cases. Interestingly for CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet the <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> remains competitive and about 5% lower compared to the baseline. This could possibly be attributed to the fact that the embeddings of the HF trained backbone have a higher variance than the single-zoo embeddings because to reconstruct models that vary in both architecture and training dataset accurately, more fine-grained information may be required. Improving the predictive performance in this setting may require going beyond a simple linear model better model non-linear relations between the embeddings and target properties. However, for CIFAR10 we observe a more significant drop in performance that was also seen in the generative results which could be attributed to the fact that CIFAR10 trained models might be less prevalent on HF compared to CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet or that the models trained on CIFAR10 exhibit higher differences in terms of accuracy while still remaining close in weight space compared to the datasets with more classes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our baseline results are divided into multiple parts. First we closely follow the experimental set-up of SANE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to validate our proposed loss normalization and compare with the results of the original SANE (see <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). To assess the performance of sampled models for our baseline when varying the dataset we train a single backbone per model zoo (CIFAR10 and CIFAR100) using the configuration detailed in <a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (SANE (MLN)). The other datasets that we sample models for are unseen during training to validate that our change to the loss normalization still allows generating models that are out of distribution. For the later experiments (<a href="#A4.SS3.SSS2" title="D.3.2 Architectures ‣ D.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3.2</span></a>) we train the baseline with the same configuration as our Hugging Face backbone (<a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, HF-Small) but still on a single model zoo (CIFAR10).</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.3.1 </span>Datasets</h4>

<figure id="A4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/resnet_18_w_baselines.png" id="A4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:439/222;" width="439" height="222" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Performance of generated ResNet-18 models with varying backbones. Here we include the performance of both baselines separately whereas in the paper we show the max performance achieved over both baselines. Furthermore we show the performance of both the small and large HF backbone. The results indicate that training on HF models is feasible and outperforms the baselines with the exception of CIFAR10.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main paper (<a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.2 Impact of HF Model Collection Composition ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), we summarize the best performance achieved by each baseline model (trained individually on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100) and compare them to our large Hugging Face-trained backbone (HF-Large), using the configuration detailed in <a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. In contrast, <a href="#A4.F5" title="In D.3.1 Datasets ‣ D.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides a more detailed view by showing the performance of both individual baselines and our smaller Hugging Face backbone (HF-Small).
These results reveal that both HF-trained backbones remain competitive across the board. The large backbone outperforms the individual baselines on four out of five datasets, with CIFAR10 being the only exception. The model-zoo trained baselines perform well in-distribution and on datasets of comparable difficulty (i.e., similar number of classes), but their generalization to different datasets is more limited. In contrast, our HF-trained backbones are able to sample effectively across diverse datasets.
Although HF-Large offers slight performance gains over HF-Small, it comes at the cost of increased training time. However, larger performance differences become apparent when sampling across architectures rather than datasets (see <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.3.2 </span>Architectures</h4>

<figure id="A4.T10" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>Performance of individual generated models after finetuning for 1-5 epochs on ImageNet-1K when sampling from the SANE baseline trained on CIFAR10 (<a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) compared to training from scratch. The baseline is competitive for architectures close to the model-zoo training set (e.g., ResNet-18,34,50 and a tiny ConvNext) but fails to scale to larger models as well as architectures less similar to those included in the training data such as transformers. For those architectures the performance is often even worse than training from scratch.</figcaption>

<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Ablations</h3>

<section id="A4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.1 </span>Masked Loss Normalization (MLN)</h4>

<figure id="A4.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:60%;"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/reconstruction_comparison_v2.png" id="A4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:329/110;" width="329" height="110" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Comparison of weight distributions of a selection of ResNet layers between original weights (blue/left) vs reconstructed weights (right). We compare reconstruction without normalization (orange), with full token normalization (green) and with masked loss normalization (red). Without normalization the weights of layers with narrow distributions are squashed towards the mean. Normalizing per-token fixes that issue. Ignoring the mask introduces a strong bias, particularly for batch-norm layers. Reconstructions with MLN match the original the closest.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further investigate whether MLN can be used as a suitable replacement for layer wise loss normalization, we evaluate the distribution of reconstructed weights vs original weights when not normalizing the loss at all, normalizing the loss per-token (including masked values) and normalizing on signal values only. After training, we use models from the test split to be reconstructed by the backbone (which corresponds to a simple forward pass through the encoder-decoder). Following previous work, we use the match of weight distribution as a proxy for how well-reconstructed models mirror the original models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>. Results are shown in Fig. <a href="#A4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ D.4.1 Masked Loss Normalization (MLN) ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Masked loss normalization achieves a more accurate alignment between the reconstructed distribution and the original weight distribution across model parameters compared to full-token normalization, see <a href="#A4.F6" title="In D.4.1 Masked Loss Normalization (MLN) ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, particularly of batch-norm layer weights. By focusing on signal values only, the masked normalization more effectively maintains the original weight distributions, reducing reconstruction error and providing a stable signal even in high-parameter regimes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.2 </span>Tokenization</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we compare the two different tokenization variants introduced in Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="Tokenization ‣ 3.3 Efficient Model Weight Processing ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>. We evaluate whether there are any significant differences in terms of pretraining and downstream performance when training on HF models. To that end, we compare the explained variance <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i}\lVert T_{i}-\hat{T}_{i}\rVert^{2}}{\sum_{i}\lVert T_{i}-\bar{T}\rVert^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msub><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msub><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i}\lVert T_{i}-\hat{T}_{i}\rVert^{2}}{\sum_{i}\lVert T_{i}-\bar{T}\rVert^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> of the reconstructed tokens to validate if our backbone converges when training on the HF dataset. As discussed previously, sparse tokenization can add substantial amounts of padding per token when tokenizing different architectures.
More specifically, after tokenization our HF model dataset includes approximately 600M tokens for the dense variation and 730M tokens using sparse tokenization (with tokensize 288). The largest model included in the HF trainset contains ~1.3B weights and is split into 5M individual tokens using sparse and 4.5M tokens using dense tokenization. Since the models have vastly different sizes, we use the number of tokens in the dataset as measure of size.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/rsq_tokenization.png" id="A4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:165/117;" width="165" height="117" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><math id="A4.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-score of reconstructed tokens on a hold-out validation set of models to assess reconstruction quality. The results indicate that dense tokenization works and shows smoother convergence.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dense tokenization matches performance while being significantly more efficient</h5>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our HF dataset, sparse tokenization introduces 20% padding per token, whereas dense tokenization adds only 0.01% padding on average. As a result, when processed by the weight-space backbone, dense tokens lead to a higher compression ratio compared to sparse tokens. To ensure a fair comparison, we adjust the token size of the dense dataset accordingly. The results in Fig. <a href="#A4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ D.4.2 Tokenization ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> show that both tokenization strategies yield similar reconstruction quality during backbone training. In addition, dense tokenization reduces disk usage by 20% relative to sparse tokenization, leading to faster training and offering a better balance between efficiency and performance. We further evaluate and discuss downstream performance of sampled models across five datasets when varying tokenization in <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Generative Results ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.02096v1/assets/img/sparse_v_dense_sampled.png" id="A4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:274/174;" width="274" height="174" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Performance of sampled models of our HF-Small backbone configuration when using sparse or dense tokenization.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A4.F8" title="In Dense tokenization matches performance while being significantly more efficient ‣ D.4.2 Tokenization ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> we show the accuracy of sampled models on the target dataset without any finetuning. To train the backbones we use the configuration as outlined in <a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. The results show higher performance when using sparse tokenization for the datasets with ten classes whereas dense tokenization shows slightly higher performance for the datasets with 100 and 200 classes. However, as mentioned in the main paper, dense tokenization is more efficient during training and we believe that the overhead introduced with sparse tokenization in terms of storage and compute is not preferable to dense tokenization overall, in particular for our training set-up with diverse architectures in the training dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.3 </span>Positional Encodings</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For evaluating the performance impact of using sinusoidal positional encodings instead of learned embeddings we train the weight space backbone in the HF-small configuration (<a href="#A3.T4" title="In Appendix C Implementation details ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) on model zoos as we cannot train of the HF dataset with learned embeddings. The results show we achieve similar performance compared to the baseline setting while only training a single backbone instead of one per dataset/architecture pair. We do observe however that in this setting we need to train for more epochs compared to using learned embeddings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T11" class="ltx_table ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">

</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>
Performance of sampled ResNet-18 models when training only on a fraction of the data. The results indicate that after a certain number of training tokens the performance saturates and does not increase significantly anymore given a constant backbone size. On the other hand, performance drops to random guessing (with the exception of EuroSAT and SVHN) when training on less than ~45M tokens showing that the number of samples included are more important than trying to restrict the models in the training data to be more similar in terms of architecture, even if we use the same architecture during training and sampling. Furthermore, training on HF data requires more samples than when training on a homogeneous model zoo, as the HF data is more noisy and possibly also contains models that are not converged or only trained for a few epochs. Nevertheless, when including enough samples training on HF is competitive and even outperforms training on homogenous model zoos in most cases.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A4.T12" title="In D.4.4 Training Dataset Composition ‣ D.4 Ablations ‣ Appendix D Additional Results &amp; Ablations ‣ Learning Model Representations Using Publicly Available Model Hubs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> we train only on the specified fraction of the dataset using a logarithmic scale from 0.01 to 0.64. For reference we also include the previous result acquired by training on the full vision transformer HF datset. The results indicate that increasing training sample count is beneficial up to a certain degree. The backbone trained on 64% of the data performs similarly or even better in some cases compared to training on the full dataset, which also serves as motivation for training a larger backbone given there is enough data available. Performance drops significantly when further restricting the number of samples and remains around random guessing when training on 24M or fewer tokens with the exception of EuroSAT and SVHN, similar to the performance of the HF ResNet trained backbone that contains 35M tokens. Therefore it is beneficial to include more samples and more diverse architectures over restricting the dataset to a single architecture class if there are not enough samples available.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
